name: Varirata National Park and the Owen Stanley foothills
blurb: Birds-of-paradise, fig trees and fruit bats above Port Moresby.

tip.title: Take away the fig trees
tip.text: Figs feed fruit bats, birds-of-paradise and pitohuis. Set Fig trees to -100% and watch the fruit eaters, then the snakes and monitors that hunt them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Fig trees bear fruit that feeds many forest birds and fruit bats. Wikipedia lists figs among the main foods of the hooded pitohui and the spectacled flying fox.
A tussock grass of open savannah and woodland. Grasses like this cover the lower, drier slopes beside the rainforest.
A large fruit bat. It eats rainforest fruit, especially figs, and eucalypt and other Myrtaceae flowers. It is the most recorded mammal in the GBIF circle.
Eats other insects and the honeydew of sap-sucking insects it tends. By deterring plant-eating insects it protects the trees it nests in.
An introduced toad. Wikipedia says it was released in New Guinea in the 1930s. It eats many invertebrates, including ants, and is itself eaten by crows and kookaburras.
An omnivore that eats invertebrates, fruit, carrion and smaller birds. GloBI records it eating cane toads, which it can kill safely.
A large tree-dwelling lizard that eats birds, small mammals, eggs, other reptiles, frogs and carrion.
Strong tropical sunshine drives plant growth in both forest and savannah.
Rain feeds the rainforest. The park mixes dense forest with drier open savannah, so the wet and dry seasons shape which plants grow where.
Nutrients recycled from dead plants and animals feed the next growth of trees and grass.
Fungi, bacteria and insects that break down dead leaves and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
